newsitem.title: USA: Write a complaint letter -- it's easy and it works.
newsitem.headline: Write a complaint letter -- it's easy and it works.

text.p: Millions of Americans buy products every year that fall apart, make funny noises or give off horrible fumes. Many consumers are able to get refunds or replacements at the store where the product was purchased; others can get the item serviced under warranty.
But there are times when all good efforts fail, and the only thing to do is go to the top -- contact the manufacturer.
The best method is to send a letter, but the thought of writing terrifies many people.

"A lot of people believe writing is difficult, but it's not. You do what the brain does when you're speaking -- plan, feed information to the mouth, clarify," said Jim Mastro, author, writer and expert on writing complaint letters.
"You have to be in the mindset to realise you've been wronged, and want redress for the wrong," he said from his home in San Diego, Calif.
A complaint letter should be the first step of last resort, he said.
Let's say you have a malfunctioning air conditioner that is only one year old.

First, make a phone call to the retailer, service company or manufacturer. Often, a phone call is all it takes to get a replacement, service for existing machine or some other redress. The company's name, address and occasionally its phone number can be found on the product itself, on the box or on instructions that come with the item.
"Phone calls can be useful, sometimes it's all it takes," Mastro said.
"But often it's difficult to articulate exactly what you want to say. You are frustrated and angry."
With a letter, "you can think, revise and modify your thoughts. It's an unemotional piece of work."
To write a complaint letter, you don't have to be a lawyer or a college professor. All you have to be is yourself.
Using a format called the "inverted pyramid," put the most important idea first, Mastro said.
First, briefly state the problem, "I bought an air conditioner one year ago and it does not work to my satisfaction."
Then briefly state what you want done, "I would like a new air conditioner to replace the defective one, or I would like my money back."
Briefly describe when and where you bought it, how much you spent and what other steps you've taken to address your problem. Make sure you include your address and phone number.
Mastro said a complaint letter should be written to the president of the company.
"To get attention, write to the person in charge." If the letter is addressed to customer service, Mastro fears "it's going into the mill."

The company's corporate executives can be found by either calling the company and asking, or by checking resource books such as the Thomas Register of Companies or the Standard & Poor's Guide, both available at public libraries.
The tone of the letter should be strong without being insulting. One advantage of letter writing is that you can edit out anger. On the phone that's hard to do.
Expect to hear back from the company either by letter or by phone within 10 working days.
If there's been no response within this time, Mastro said, write a second letter, indicating that you're getting even more upset and give them just one week to respond.

No response? Now it's time to get out the big guns -- contact a third party such as a lawyer, or representative from a consumer organisation, government agency or the attorney general in the area where the company is located. In a third letter, tell the company you've done so.
Another good tactic at this point is to contact local print or broadcast media, Mastro said.
"The best help often comes from the media -- radio, TV or newspapers. The last thing a company wants is to be on the air in a bad light."
Generally, 85 percent of first letters get a response, he said, and 99 percent of consumer complaints are solved by the second letter.
Whenever possible, always type your letter or use a word processor. You want the product to look credible so use only white paper and a business-sized envelope.
"You have to be flexible in your redress," Mastro said. "You have to weigh the pluses and minuses... Don't be unreasonable."

Mastro and Patricia H. Westheimer have written "How to Write Complaint Letters that Work -- a consumer's guide to resolving conflicts and getting results" (Park Ave. Productions, JIST Works Inc. $12.95). For more information on the book, call 1-800-547-8872.
